Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:115: Behold, it said, "and then the Holy One, blessed be He, is found full of blessings every day" - and along these lines is the matter of the Grace After Meals, which causes the bestowal of blessings to the Shechinah. And in passing, the merit of one who asks for his sustenance every day is explained - that he is called a "son," and it is the way of a son to love his father, and this love is that he causes the bestowal of blessings above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:116: And further it explained shortly after that concerning those who ask for their sustenance every day from the Holy One, blessed be He, it is said (Psalms 147:11), "the LORD favors those who fear Him, those who wait for His kindness" - and they, of blessed memory, said in brief: and who are "those who fear Him," from whom this favor emerges? It then says, "those who wait for His kindness" - those who watch and wait every single day to ask for their sustenance from the Holy One, blessed be He - as implied by "those who wait for His kindness" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:117: Further, in the Zohar (Parashat Miketz, page 199b), it opened and said the verse following it, (Proverbs 28:20), "a faithful man abounds with blessings" - this is one who has faith in the Holy One, blessed be He, such as Rabbi Yesa the Elder, who, even though he had food to eat that day, would not prepare it until he asked for his sustenance before the Holy King; after he prayed his prayer and asked for his sustenance before the King, then he would prepare it, and he would always say, we shall not prepare until it is given from the King's house - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:118: And there are some who err and say that the blessing "Barech Aleinu" is the entirety of asking for sustenance, but from this teaching there is proof against them, for it said "after he prayed his prayer and asked for his sustenance" - it appears that the matter of prayer is one matter in itself, and asking for sustenance is another matter in itself.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:119: And similar to this they said in Midrash Tanchuma (Beshalach 20), and likewise in the Mechilta, on the verse (Exodus 16:4), "behold, I shall rain down for you," and so on, "a portion for each day" - they, of blessed memory, said, whoever created the day created its sustenance; from here Rabbi Eliezer of Modi'im would say, whoever has what to eat today and says, what shall I eat tomorrow, is among those of little faith - to this point. And so they said in Tractate Sotah (48b), on the verse "and the men of faith have ceased" - Rabbi Yitzchak said, these are people who believe in the Holy One, blessed be He. It was taught: Rabbi Eliezer the Great says, whoever has bread in his basket and says, what shall I eat tomorrow, is only among those of little faith - and this is what Rabbi Elazar said, what is meant by (Zechariah 4:10), "for who has despised the day of small things?" - what caused the righteous that their table will be squandered [not fully rewarded] in the future to come? The smallness that was in them, that they did not believe in the Holy One, blessed be He - to this point. And Rashi, peace be upon him, explained: those who believe in the Holy One, blessed be He, to part with their money for the beautification of a mitzvah, for charity, and for the expenses of Sabbaths and festivals - "their table shall be squandered in the future to come," meaning they do not receive full reward, and this is the meaning of "who has despised the day" that shall come upon the righteous, [because of] the smallness of those of little faith - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:120: And just as a person should not eat until he has prayed for his sustenance, so he should not eat until he has occupied himself with Torah and studied at the fixed hour for his study - and so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained in the Midrash Bamidbar Rabbah, Parashat Nazir, on the verse (Ecclesiastes 10:17), "happy are you, O land, whose king is a free man" - explaining it of one occupied with Torah, who is called a free man, since Torah is called freedom - and it says afterward, "and your princes eat at the proper time" - that they set fixed times for Torah and afterward eat, to fulfill what is said (ibid. 9:7), "go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart, for God has already favored your deeds" - this is what is written after it (ibid. 10:17), "for strength, and not for drunkenness" - for the strength of Torah, and not for the drinking of wine - to this point, relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:121: And although we have explained the general intent of eating, it remains to explain it in particular, for we are obligated to unify [the divine Names] above in all things, along the lines of "let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven" (Avot, chapter 2, mishnah 12), and likewise "know Him in all your ways" (Proverbs 3:6), as explained in the Gate of Love. And this was the merit of the Patriarchs, that even in physical deeds they would unify - and the proof is the matter of the wells of water that Abraham and Isaac dug, which is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Toldot, page 141a), that their matter was like the mitzvah of tefillin for us - to this point; see there. And likewise Jacob, in the matter of the rods that he peeled at the watering troughs, which is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayetze, page 162a, Sitrei Torah) to have had the intent of laying tefillin - these are its words: Jacob, the perfect one, took those rods, [alluding to] the tefillin of the head; "at the troughs" - he found and set a place for the space of the tefillin - to this point. And so, in the matter of eating in its particulars, there is a complete unification, as we shall explain.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:122: And Rabbeinu Bachya, of blessed memory, wrote in Sefer Shulchan Shel Arba (Second Gate) concerning the matter of eating, something fitting for unification - these are its words: you already know that the survival of the soul is not through the eating of the body, and its actions are not revealed except through the body, and from this you shall understand the matter of the sacrifices, which is from the secrets of Torah, of which it is written (Numbers 28:2), "for My fire-offerings, a pleasing aroma to Me" - and does the power of the supernal soul increase and add to the fire-offerings by their consumption of the sacrifices? And so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said, "My offering, My food for My fire-offerings" - one might think, "My food," therefore Scripture says, "for My fire-offerings" - it is to My fire-offerings that you give - and this is because of the soul's binding within the attributes: the powers of the soul are bound with the powers of the body. And understand the verse that the sweet singer [David] mentioned (Psalms 103:1), "bless the LORD, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless His holy Name" - he unified the hidden with the hidden and the revealed with the revealed - and this acquisition is that the powers of the soul are not revealed and do not come into action except through the body; if so, the body is a great necessity for publicizing the greatness of the soul and its perfection. And you should know that a person's eating is only an illusion - it is not a true thing nor a certain action, for it is a false thing and a changing matter, passing through the intermediate organs from one cause to another; but the pure thoughts in wisdom and the cleaving of thought to the light of intellect in the wisdom of Chokhmah - that is the enduring, certain eating, along the lines of what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, expounded (Vayikra Rabbah 20:6), "and they beheld God, and ate and drank" (Exodus 24:11) - Rabbi Yochanan said, this is certain eating, as it is said (Proverbs 16:15), "in the light of the king's face is life."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:123: And he said shortly after: therefore, when he eats, he must free his thought and let it roam toward the Holy One, blessed be He, over every single mouthful, along the lines of "and they beheld God, and ate and drank" - and this is similar to what the Sages, of blessed memory, expounded (Bereishit Rabbah 14:12), "let every soul [neshamah] praise the LORD" (Psalms 150:6) - for every breath [neshimah], give Him praise. And you can learn this from the generation of the wilderness, for when they ate the manna their intent would roam toward the Shechinah, and they would intend humility - for this is why wisdom required that the measure of their food be an omer, which is a tenth of an ephah, meaning one part in ten of an ephah, along the reasoning of the mitzvah of tithing - for when a person measures nine measures and separates the tenth, the wise shall contemplate the tenth, which is the attribute that "gives prey to her household" and provides sustenance for every created being above and below - and for this reason they said (Berachot 47b), "nine and a minor combine," meaning they combine for the blessing over food, to bless, "let us bless our God," He being the Master who provides sustenance to every creature.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:124: And he said further shortly after: you thus learn that when a person stands at his table and eats with this thought, behold, that eating, though a bodily matter and a natural action, returns to become an intellectual, ascending service - and this is the reason it is written (Proverbs 3:6), "in all your ways, know Him," as I have mentioned - and if so, his eating is considered a complete service, like one of the divine services or like one of the commandments - to this point, relevant here. And we have shortened his words to what is needed for our intent, and skipped what is not essential.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:125: And it appears to us, according to what is included in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Zohar and in the Ra'aya Meheimna, that one must intend that the food is bestowed from the side of the right to the attribute of Tzaddik [Righteous One], and the Tzaddik bestows it to Tzedek [Righteousness], food from the side of the right - so it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah, end of page 168) concerning "upon the land and upon the food" - these are its words: "upon the land" - this is the land of the living; "and upon the food" - this is Chesed; behold, this is included with that in one bond - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:126: And there (Parashat Vayechi, page 240a), concerning (Judges 14:14), "out of the eater came forth food" - it explains that from the Tzaddik, who is called "the eater," food goes forth to the lower attribute, which is the Shechinah - these are its words: he opened and said, "out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness" - this verse has support for us: "out of the eater" - this is the Tzaddik, as it is written (Proverbs 13:25), "the Tzaddik eats to satisfy his soul" - the Tzaddik certainly eats and takes everything; why? "To satisfy his soul" - to give satiety to that which is called "his soul," which is called David. "Came forth food" - for were it not for that Tzaddik, food would never go forth, and the world would not be able to endure through it - to this point. And it seems to me that MA'ACHAL [food] equals 91 in gematria, corresponding to the two Names unified in Tzaddik - and likewise, food is bestowed from the secret of unification, as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayechi, page 240a) on the verse (Psalms 104:15), "and bread sustains man's heart" - that the word "u'lechem" [and bread] is along the lines of Vav-Hei; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:127: Further, there (Zohar, Parashat Vayikra, page 11b), concerning the explanation of the Name Shaddai in Tzaddik - it explains that He is called Shaddai because He gives sufficient [dai] provision of food to the worlds - these are its words: the ninth is Shaddai, who says to the world, "enough" [dai] - for it is sufficiency, and sufficiency comes to the world only from the Tzaddik, who is the Foundation [Yesod] of the world, who says to the world, "enough" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:128: If so, one must intend that just as the supernal attribute of Tzaddik eats to give satiety to his supernal soul, the soul of David, so he takes the flow from the Tzaddik from the side of the right and from the attribute of Tzedek, to give sustenance to his own lower soul, which is a portion of the Shechinah - and this is along the lines of what is explained in the Zohar, Parashat Vayera (page 100b), "who has not lifted up his soul in vain" (Psalms 24:4) - it is written "nafshi" [my soul] - and we have copied its words in the Gate of Love (chapter 11).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:129: And through this we shall understand what Hillel, peace be upon him, used to say to his students, "come, let us perform an act of kindness for the guest" - and he said that this is the poor soul, and we have copied it in the Gate of Love (chapter 11). And this is because the bestowal of food is from the side of Chesed, and therefore it is called an act of kindness [gemilut chasadim].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:130: Now, the soul dwells in the heart, as explained in the Tikkunim (page 49a), which we copied above in chapter 1 - it follows that the soul, in this aspect that dwells in the heart, which is fire, is [subject to] judgment - and therefore one must bestow food upon it from the side of the right and quiet its judgments, for on a fast day, when there is no food, a person's fat is consumed by the heat of the heart. And afterward he shall remember to give it food to eat for the fire resting upon his head - the secret of (Deuteronomy 4:24), "for the LORD your God is a consuming fire" - and what is its eating? Torah and mitzvot, and this is (Ecclesiastes 9:8), "and let oil not be lacking on your head," as explained above in the Gate of Love (chapter 4) - and therefore he should occupy himself with Torah before the Grace After Meals, as explained, and the Grace After Meals is a positive commandment, and through this the supernal fire eats - and this is why they were strict in Parashat Vayakhel (page 218a-b) concerning the Grace After Meals, because it is a repair for the Shechinah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:131: Further, he should intend what is explained in the Ra'aya Meheimna (page 236a), that Netzach and Hod are called "millstones" [tochanot] from the side of the right, and are called two Vavs of the esophagus [vashet] from the side of the left - these are its words: Netzach and Hod are two halves of the body, like two twins, and therefore they are called "clouds" [shechakim], the two of them as one - the two Vavs are from the esophagus, from the side of the left, and they are the two millstones of the side of the right - to this point, relevant here. And it is possible that they are called "millstones" from the side of the right, since there are the thirty-two paths there, and the millstones, included in the thirty-two, separate the waste from the food - see Parashat Pekudei. And it is possible that they are called the two Vavs of the esophagus because the esophagus has two skins, the outer one red and the inner one white. Now, he should intend that just as above, before the flow comes to Tzaddik and Tzedek, it is prepared through the millstones and through the esophagus, so he grinds through his millstones [teeth] and swallows through his esophagus, to give sustenance to his soul, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:132: Now, the lower man differs from the supernal man in one respect: the supernal man, the supernal flow is bestowed within him from the brain to the heart and from the heart to the liver, as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah, page 153a); but the lower man needs to refine his food through the stomach, and the food comes to the liver, and the liver distributes food to all the organs, and offers the choicest of the blood to the heart, and the choicest of the choicest of all ascends to the brain, which are the vapors from the food, being the finest part. And the reason for this is that man, because of his physicality, needs two aspects: first, that the flow come also to his mouth, and he grind it until it is refined through all the vessels mentioned, and afterward, from below upward, it ascends to the heart and to the brain, as explained. But above it is the opposite, for above, in the brain, it is very fine, and it needs to descend from level to level until it thickens and becomes fit for those below to receive it. And there is no aspect of the food returning from below to above except on a fast day, when the lower man's food has already been digested and the physical blood has been drawn near to the heart, and after it has already been digested, a person offers his fat to the supernal liver, which is the tenth attribute, and from there to the heart, and from there to the brain (Zohar, ibid.) - and we shall explain their matter in the topic of fasting.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:133: And my teacher, peace be upon him, wrote concerning the mitzvah of "and you shall eat and be satisfied" (Deuteronomy 8:10), that one should intend, in the matter of eating, the binding of all the holy [sefirot] from below to above, in the secret of (Numbers 28:2), "a fire-offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD." And I add that just as the body is built from four elements, and food gives strength to the four physical elements, so, since the soul's foundation is the four letters of YHVH, the secret of (Ezekiel 37:9), "from the four winds, come, O breath" - as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Shemot, page 13b) - it too enjoys from that food; and therefore in the Grace After Meals there are four blessings, corresponding to the four ruling chariots, as explained in the Zohar, and which we have copied above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:134: Further, it is fitting to intend in eating that everything a person eats has a holy inwardness, and chaff and straw mixed within it because of the sin of Adam - and through the grinding it is separated, and his soul enjoys from the inwardness within it, which becomes blood, while the chaff and straw within it become the residue bestowed to the external forces - and since it becomes foul, certainly the good that was in it has already been separated out, and what remains is refuse to be cast outside; and therefore one who delays relieving himself transgresses "you shall not make your souls detestable" (Leviticus 11:43), as explained, of blessed memory (Makkot 16b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:135: Further, when he takes something from the table in his right hand to bless, he should intend that he raises it up from the world of the female to the world of the male. And in drinking water he should intend to cool the judgment of the heart and the stomach, since water is bestowed from Chesed - and MAYIM [water] equals 90, and with the word itself, 91, corresponding to YAHDONHY [the unified Names] - it follows that they are the unification of the two Names from the side of Chesed. And further he should intend the four Names, AB, SAG, MAH, BAN, which have nine Yuds, corresponding to MAYIM - and there is a further secret in this. And all water comes to the lung, and the secret of the lung is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Pinchas, page 236a) to be the Seraphim, and the Seraphim are at the Throne, as it is written (Isaiah 6:2), "seraphim stood above Him, six wings for each one" - and it is explained in the Tikkunim (page 26a) that this is the secret of the Name of forty-two [letters], for there are six letters for each Name, and the Seraphim stand to cool the fire of the heart, which is the Shechinah, which is judgment.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:136: And one who conducts his eating in the manner we have written is found to be as one standing before the Holy One, blessed be He, and shall not come to be a glutton at his table, for he stands before the supernal King and shall not come to treat himself lightly - and awe and humility shall be drawn upon him, and then his eating is not to fill his desire, for one who eats to fill his desire removes from himself awe and shame and draws upon himself external desire, and then all his eating is on the side of the evil inclination, to inflame him and cause him to sin - unlike one who thinks that he eats before the Holy One, blessed be He, and that there is no partition separating between him and the Holy One, blessed be He, for behold he stands and blesses, "Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe," as one speaking directly to his fellow, and it is fitting to be careful of what comes out of his mouth, and not remove awe from himself.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:137: And it is fitting to think of His great kindness, that He did good with him to bestow that food upon him, since from the side of his own deeds he was not worthy of food, for "the soul that sins, it shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4) - but rather it is His kindness that sustains the wicked and the good alike.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:138: And when he thinks of his evil deeds, he shall not come to indulge in delight during the six weekdays, as it is said (Job 3:24), "for my sighing comes before my bread" - and these are the words of the Shechinah, when she is, as it were, in exile; and during the six weekdays, when she is called "poor," he should conduct his eating like a poor man - and this is called (Psalms 146:5), "whose hope is in the LORD his God" - and it is enough for the servant to be like his master. But on the Sabbath day he shall indulge in delight, for through his delight he fulfills the mitzvah of "and you shall call the Sabbath a delight" (Isaiah 58:13), and there is no exile on the Sabbath - and he should intend that all his delight is bestowed above in the secret of "Eden, river, garden," as explained in the Zohar, Parashat Yitro.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:139: Also, it is fitting to conduct the matter of eating at a specific hour, namely the sixth hour, the time of the meal of Torah scholars, as they, of blessed memory, explained (Pesachim 12b). And the reason for this is that the attribute of the day is [like] a Torah scholar: it is divided, half to Chesed and half to Gevurah, and the portion of Chesed is the first six hours - and therefore the Torah scholar, who holds the middle line, holds fast to the end of Chesed before the side of Gevurah begins, which is what lies between the two. And in the earlier hours he should intend to give food to his soul, as explained above, as it is written (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul," after his soul has already been satisfied from Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:140: And concerning the quality of food, he should conduct himself according to the Torah, which said (Exodus 16:8), "when the LORD gives you in the evening meat to eat, and bread in the morning to be satisfied" - and Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "meat to eat" and not "to be satisfied" - Torah taught proper conduct, that one should not eat meat to satiety. And why did it see fit to bring down bread in the morning and meat in the evening? Because they asked for bread properly, since a person cannot be without bread, but they asked for meat improperly, since they could have been without meat. And this teaching is brought in Yoma (75), and it says there, from here Torah taught proper conduct, that a person should eat meat only at night - to this point. And all these matters have an allusion and a secret, for meat, which is red, alludes to the attribute of judgment, and it is fitting that it be eaten at night, which is the attribute of judgment, and bread in the morning, which is the attribute of day, mercy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:141: And we can say that although it said that meat should be eaten only at night, this does not mean specifically nighttime, but rather the same law applies from the time of Minchah Ketanah onward, which is considered night according to Rabbi Yehudah for praying the evening prayer, and the halachah follows him - for they said in Berachot (27a), whoever acts like this master [does properly], and whoever acts like that master [does properly], and so on. And through this the language of the verse is precise, which says, "at twilight you shall eat meat," and does not say "at night." And one who does not fast, and whose custom is to rise at midnight to occupy himself with Torah - this way is fitting for him, that there be time for the digestion of the meat, and that sleep not increase for him when he rises to occupy himself with Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:142: And after we have explained the essence of the intent of eating and drinking, according to what we have been taught from Heaven and what we found in the books, we shall explain the repairs of the table, which are ten things, as explained in the Midrash Ruth (Zohar Chadash, Midrash HaNe'elam), of blessed memory: in the Grace After Meals there are known matters. One, to arrange the table in accordance with that occasion - so much so that setting the table is praiseworthy, as one who sits to eat before the King, as it is written (Deuteronomy 14:23), "and you shall eat before the LORD your God." Second, washing the hands: whoever eats without washing his hands is as though he ate impurity. Third, [the manner of] washing the hands: he should wash the right with the left, and the left shall serve the right, and he should wash up to the joint measure that the Sages decreed. Fourth, he must raise his hands after washing, at the time he blesses, and join the two arms together as one at the time of raising his hands. Fifth, he must juxtapose the blessing to the washing. Sixth, to give a piece of bread to a poor person. Seventh, to bless the blessing of HaMotzi and be precise in it, and it is forbidden to eat without a blessing. Eighth, one who eats at his table must not be a glutton or a guzzler, but rather eat as one eating before the King. Ninth, there must be words of Torah at his table, and a lone individual who has no one with whom to occupy himself in Torah, it suffices for him with his blessings. Tenth, the final waters [after the meal] are obligatory, though they did not require a blessing over them - to this point, relevant here. And some of these repairs are explained in the Ra'aya Meheimna, Parashat Pinchas (page 245a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:143: Concerning the arranging of the table, aside from what was explained, that it be as one eating before the King, it is also because of the honor of the bread, which one must treat with honor, as we shall copy its words concerning HaMotzi. And so they said in the Zohar (Parashat Pinchas, page 244a), the section "and a tenth of an ephah" - and it said, why "a tenth of an ephah"? Rather, "a tenth of an ephah" corresponds to Knesset Yisrael, which is the tenth of the levels, and needs to be given between the two arms, and it is the fine flour of bread and it is bread - and because it is bread, it is not counted among the bread of the seven species, which is wheat, barley, spelt, and so on, [governed by] the appointed [angel] of the world; no appointed one is set over them but the Holy One, blessed be He, alone - and therefore whoever treats bread with contempt and throws it on the ground, poverty pursues him, and one appointed one is charged with this, and it pursues him to give him poverty, and he shall not leave the world until he needs to depend on creatures - and of him it is written (Job 15:23), "he wanders about for bread, where is it?" - "he wanders about," and he goes about, moving and exiled from place to place [seeking] "where is bread?" and there is no one who takes notice of him - this is what is written, "where" - where is one who has mercy on him, so that he not be forgotten - to this point. Behold, it is explicit that one must treat bread with honor, because it is supervised by the Shechinah and not by other princes and appointed ones.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:144: And concerning the second [repair], the washing of hands, it says in the Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas, page 245) - these are its words: second, the washing of hands, up to the measure the Sages decreed, for there are five knuckles with fourteen joints [in the hand], and likewise there are fourteen joints of the left hand, and they are twenty-eight joints, corresponding to the twenty-eight [numerical value of the word] KO'ACH [strength] of YHVH, corresponding to the twenty-eight letters of the first verse of the account of Creation, of which it is said (Numbers 14:17), "and now, please, let the strength [ko'ach] of my Lord be great" - and the ten fingers allude to the ten utterances of the account of Creation - and therefore the masters of the Mishnah established that whoever treats the washing of hands with contempt is uprooted from the world; why? Because within it is the secret of the ten utterances and the twenty-eight letters by which the world was created - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:145: And concerning the seventh [repair], to bless the blessing of HaMotzi, it says there in Midrash Ruth - these are its words: for so said Rav Hamnuna the Elder, there are seven lands, and all of them are dwelt in below, but of all of them the Holy One, blessed be He, chose only this inhabited world, and of all of them, of those seven species, they are found only in this inhabited world, and in all of them the Holy One, blessed be He, gives all the grasses and all the produce of the land except these seven species of bread for human beings - and therefore one must be precise about it, for bread is entrusted into His own hand and not into the hand of any other appointed one, and He is the one who brings it forth and no other - and therefore "HaMotzi" [He who brings forth] and not "motzi" [one who brings forth] - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:146: And in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 16) it says that the Hei of "HaMotzi" is the Shechinah, and one must intend to separate from the chaff and straw, which are the husks - for just as wheat has chaff and straw exempt from tithing, and the wheat, once separated from them, is obligated in tithing - these are its words in brief: and therefore, in "HaMotzi," through the Hei with the Bet, one must be precise about the Hei, that it be clean without refuse - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:147: The eighth [repair], not to be a glutton, is explained in Midrash Ruth - these are its words: eighth, that he not be a glutton and guzzler, but rather as one eating before the King, for blessing does not rest in the innards of one found to be a gorging guzzler, as it is written (Genesis 25:30), "let me gulp down, please, some of that red, red stuff" - it teaches gulping. Why? Because the evil serpent rests in his innards and is not satisfied, and moreover he is called wicked, as it is written (Proverbs 13:25), "and the belly of the wicked shall want" - not have enough to be satisfied - therefore one should intend, when eating, as one who sits before the King - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:148: And the rest of the repairs of the table - giving from one's bread to the poor, and occupying oneself with words of Torah at the table, and the final waters - have been explained above. And what it said concerning words of Torah, that if he is alone he is exempt from words of Torah, it appears that the Zohar disagrees with this in Parashat Terumah (page 153b), as we have copied its words above, where it said, a table upon which words of Torah were not said, it is forbidden to bless over that table - stated without qualification, not distinguishing between an individual and several people - and therefore it is proper to be strict and say some psalm or mishnah or the like; one who fears Heaven fulfills the obligation for all of them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:149: And the pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz wrote, concerning the mishnah of three who ate at one table (Avot, chapter 3, mishnah 4) - these are its words: and Rashbam, of blessed memory, explained that Scripture opens with the altar and concludes with the table, to say that when the Temple stood, a person was atoned through the sacrifices and the song of the Levites; now, in place of the sacrifice, he feeds the poor, and in place of the song, he speaks words of Torah. And some are accustomed to sing hymns or psalms after the meal, and this is a fine custom to be spared punishment, but the essential speech is truly to say some halachic ruling or novel insight on a verse or an aggadah, for there are three categories: the wholly righteous - this is what we said; the intermediate - the psalm; the wicked - nothing at all. And just as one who does not speak words of Torah draws upon himself the power of impurity, so one who speaks words of Torah draws upon himself the power of purity, as it is written (Ezekiel 41:22), "and he said to me, this is the table."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:150: And he wrote further shortly after: and the time of eating tests and refines, to know whether one loves the Torah or not - a parable of a person who has a son overseas, that at the time of his joy he shall remember him, as Scripture says (Psalms 137:6), "if I do not set Jerusalem above my chief joy" - therefore, at the time of eating, when a person is joyful, if he remembers the Torah it shows that its love is bound in his heart, and when he forgets it because of the food, then the inclination is inflamed and grows strong in its stand, and the intellect stumbles and falls - like a parable of two fighting one another, and one falls and the other rises, for from then on he has no recovery - and because of this, the glory and beauty of the Torah shall be withheld from him from then on. And the time of the meal is a dangerous crossing, for if he then follows after the inclination, Amalek grows strong, but if he raises his hand with the Torah of Moses, Israel grows strong - to this point. It appears from his words, and so I have seen it written, that even while he is chewing the food he must reflect upon words of Torah, besides the words of Torah at the table - and so it is fitting to be strict.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:151: And concerning the repairs of the table, they elaborated at length there in the Ra'aya Meheimna (pages 245 and 246), and we have not copied its words so as not to be lengthy. And further, they explained there the repairs of the cup. And in Parashat Eikev (page 272b) the repairs of the Sabbath eve table are explained; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:152: And concerning the Grace After Meals, it is fitting that he think, when he blesses, that he thereby fulfills a positive commandment, and therefore he must not bless with a light head or drowsily, without intent, but rather prepare himself to meet his God and bless with his head covered - and for us, "covered" means that he blesses wearing the headwear he customarily wears when going out to the marketplace before other people. And he should bless with awe and love, as with all commandments requiring awe and love - and "awe" is explained in its place as fearing one's Master, who is great and dominant, and so on (page 11b) - and "love" is that he remember the great kindness that the Name did with him, and that He did good with him to prepare his sustenance for him, even though he was not worthy of this because of his sins - and this is the meaning of saying "who sustains the whole world in His goodness, with grace, with kindness, and with mercy," and so on - meaning that in His kindness He sustains all, both the wicked and the good.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:153: And he should take to heart the secret of "Ishmael, My son, bless Me" (Berachot 7a) - for although He, blessed and exalted be He, has no need of us, since He created the heavens and the heaven of heavens, the earth and all that is in it, and all need Him and He needs none of them - nevertheless, His desire is to be blessed through those below, so that they have preparation to be bestowed from His goodness; therefore it is fitting for us, His children, to do the will of our Father, to bless Him with desire and love, and to bless word by word, calmly and deliberately, to give Him praise, along the lines of "You gave our fathers a desirable land, a covenant, and a Torah," and so on. And he should bless in a loud voice, meaning that the members of his household hear his voice, so that he not bless in a whisper - for saying blessings aloud arouses the intent and brings remembrance, whether on Rosh Chodesh he shall remember "Ya'aleh V'yavo," or on the Sabbath, "Retzeh," and the like - and one who says it in a whisper forgets everything, along the lines of what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said concerning the occupation with Torah, that one must articulate it with the mouth, as it is said (Proverbs 4:22), "for they are life to those who find them" - and likewise, "ordered in all things and secured" (II Samuel 23:5), as they expounded in Eruvin (54a) - and so it is concerning blessings as well.
